statement: The seventy weeks run on without a break. The Messiah is 'cut off' within the seventieth week at the cross, and it is he who 'confirms a covenant with many' (the new covenant) and makes sacrifice cease by his once-for-all offering. The six goals of Daniel 9:24 (atonement, everlasting righteousness, anointing the most holy) are achieved in Christ's first coming. The desolation of Jerusalem in AD 70 is the announced consequence of rejecting him.
note: Postmillennialists differ on the start date (Cyrus, Artaxerxes) and on whether AD 70 falls inside or just after the seventieth week.

statement: The numbers are symbolic: seventy sevens form a jubilee-shaped period of redemption centred on Christ. Christ is the anointed one who confirms the covenant. In the influential reading of Meredith Kline, the seventieth week begins with his ministry and its second half extends through the church age, matching Revelation's 'time, times and half a time'. There is no dispensational parenthesis. The church age is part of the prophecy, not an interruption of it.
note: Many amillennialists (E. J. Young and much older Reformed exegesis) hold the more chronological 'fulfilled in Christ' view shared with postmillennialists. Some older amillennial commentators (Keil, Leupold) placed a final Antichrist at the end of a symbolic scheme.

statement: Many historic premillennialists see the prince who makes the covenant and sets up the abomination in Daniel 9:27 as an eschatological Antichrist, so at least part of the final week lies in the future. Jesus' use of Daniel in the Olivet Discourse and Paul's 'man of lawlessness' point to a final crisis before the return. They do not adopt the dispensational doctrine of a church-age parenthesis that separates Israel's programme from the church's.
note: Historic premillennialists vary widely. Posttribulationists such as Robert Gundry keep a future seventieth week, while others accept a messianic fulfilment of Daniel 9 and locate the future tribulation in other texts.

statement: Sixty-nine weeks (483 years) ran exactly to Messiah the Prince, who was then 'cut off' after them. Daniel 9:26 places the destruction of the city before the seventieth week, which requires an interval. The 'he' of Daniel 9:27 is the coming prince, the Antichrist, who makes a seven-year covenant with Israel. Because the prophecy concerns Daniel's people and city, the seventieth week resumes after the church age as the future tribulation.
note: Dispensationalists differ in chronology. Sir Robert Anderson and Harold Hoehner counted 'prophetic years' of 360 days to reach Palm Sunday. Progressive dispensationalists keep the future seventieth week but soften the Israel/church parenthesis.

statement: Daniel's prophecy is a unified, unbroken countdown, and inserting a two-thousand-year gap breaks its natural reading. The Messiah's death in the midst of the final week confirms the new covenant and ends the sacrificial system. The 'desolator' who comes on the wing of abominations is Rome in the Jewish War, and Jesus explicitly links this to his own generation.
note: Some partial preterists stretch the seventieth week to AD 70 itself, while Gentry treats AD 70 as the consequence of events within the week. Amillennial partial preterists may prefer a symbolic count.

statement: The seventy weeks were determined to 'seal up vision and prophet', so all prophecy, including resurrection and judgment, had to be fulfilled when the seventy weeks ended. That end was the destruction of the city and sanctuary in AD 70, which Daniel 12:7 ties to the shattering of the holy people's power. To leave any part of the six goals of Daniel 9:24 unfulfilled is to break the prophecy's own time limit.
note: Full preterists vary in how they count the weeks. Critics from every other school reply that 'sealing up vision' refers to Christ fulfilling and authenticating prophecy at his first coming, not to the end of all prophetic fulfilment.

statement: On the day-year principle, the seventy weeks are 490 literal years running from Artaxerxes' decree in 457 BC (Ezra 7). Week 69 ends with Christ's baptism (AD 27). He is cut off in the middle of the seventieth week (AD 31), and the week closes c. AD 34 when the gospel turns to the Gentiles. Historicists cite this precise fulfilment as the clearest confirmation of their method.
note: The 457 BC to AD 34 scheme is characteristic of Seventh-day Adventist and older Protestant historicism, though the exact crucifixion year and termini are debated.

statement: Revelation's forty-two months and 1,260 days are the two halves of Daniel's seventieth week, which is therefore still future. The first sixty-nine weeks were fulfilled literally up to Messiah, so the last must be fulfilled just as literally. Jesus placed the 'abomination of desolation' immediately before his coming, which locates it at the end of the age.
note: Most futurists are dispensational and hold the parenthesis view. Historic-premillennial and pre-wrath futurists also keep a future seventieth week without that framework.

statement: Biblical numbers are theological, not chronological: seventy sevens signal the complete span of God's redemptive work. Revelation reuses Daniel's half-week ('time, times and half a time') to describe the whole period between Christ's ascension and return, during which the church is protected yet persecuted. The prophecy therefore portrays the church's present age rather than a future timetable.
note: Idealism is primarily a way of reading Revelation, so idealists differ on Daniel 9 itself. Many adopt the standard messianic fulfilment while reading Revelation's half-week symbolically.

statement: Daniel 9 is fulfilled in Christ, whose death confirms the covenant. Its 'half-week' becomes in Revelation a symbol of the church's whole tribulation-filled era between the first and second comings. Many eclectic readers also allow for an intensified final phase of that period just before the end, so the pattern is both already fulfilled and yet to culminate.
note: Eclectic interpreters (Beale, Osborne, Keener) weight the futurist element differently.

statement: Most contemporary postmillennial writers hold that John wrote before AD 70, during Nero's persecution. The temple is still standing to be measured (Revelation 11:1-2), five kings have fallen and the sixth now reigns (Revelation 17:10), and the book insists its events are 'near'. On this view the main judgment scenes lie in our past, which leaves the future open for the gospel's advance.
note: Disputed. Older postmillennialists such as Jonathan Edwards, Charles Hodge and B. B. Warfield accepted the traditional Domitianic date and read Revelation historicistically or symbolically. Postmillennialism as a millennial view does not depend on the early date.

statement: Most amillennial scholars accept the late date of c. AD 95, following Irenaeus's statement that the vision was seen near the end of Domitian's reign. Imperial cult pressure, the decline of the Ephesian church's first love and the established Christian presence at Laodicea fit the 90s. Because amillennialists read Revelation as a recapitulating portrayal of the whole church age, their view does not depend on the date.
note: Disputed. A minority of amillennialists, notably Jay Adams in The Time Is at Hand, hold the early date and read much of Revelation preteristically.

statement: Historic premillennialists generally accept the traditional late date (c. AD 95) on the strength of Irenaeus, Eusebius and the internal picture of the churches. Revelation was written to churches facing Domitian's pressure, and it prophesies the final conflict and Christ's coming rather than the events of AD 70.
note: Disputed. Ladd's commentary accepted the late date. Because historic premillennialists usually read Revelation futuristically or eclectically, the date carries little interpretive weight for them.

statement: Revelation was written c. AD 95, as Irenaeus (a disciple of Polycarp, who knew John) testifies and as the early church uniformly reported. Since it was written after AD 70, it cannot be a prophecy of Jerusalem's fall, and its judgments remain future. Dispensational writers regard the early date as an argument made to rescue preterism.
note: Disputed. Dispensationalists sometimes add that even an early date would not by itself prove preterism.

statement: Revelation was written before AD 70, most likely c. AD 65-66 while Nero reigned. The temple still stands (Revelation 11:1-2), and the sixth king 'is' (Revelation 17:10), on most counts Nero. The number 666 fits Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters, and the book repeatedly says its events are 'soon'. Irenaeus's sentence is ambiguous and may say that John, not the vision, was seen in Domitian's time.
note: Disputed. Most partial preterists treat the early date as essential. A minority of preterist-leaning readers accept the late date and apply Revelation to the fall of pagan Rome instead. Opponents note that the majority of New Testament scholars favour c. 95.

statement: Revelation must predate AD 70, because its 'soon' and 'near' language (Revelation 1:1, Revelation 1:3, Revelation 22:6-20) promises the Parousia within the lifetime of its first readers. The temple of Revelation 11 still stands, and the great city 'where their Lord was crucified' (Revelation 11:8) is Jerusalem, whose judgment the book announces.
note: Disputed. Full preterists borrow most of their dating arguments from partial preterists such as Gentry, who rejects their wider conclusions.

statement: Classical historicists (Barnes, Elliott) accepted the c. AD 96 date. They read Revelation as a panorama of church history running from John's day to the end, beginning with the fall of pagan Rome and continuing through the rise of the papacy and Islam. On this reading the late date fits the sequence of seals and trumpets that follow.
note: Disputed. Historicism needs no particular date, but its classic exponents assumed the late one.

statement: Revelation was written c. AD 95 under Domitian, as the earliest external testimony (Irenaeus) states and as later fathers repeated. Since it postdates Jerusalem's fall, chapters 4-22 cannot describe AD 70 and must concern the end of the age. Futurists see the early-date case as resting on contested internal inferences.
note: Disputed. The late date is the majority view in modern New Testament scholarship, a point futurists often stress.

statement: Because Revelation portrays timeless spiritual realities, such as the conflict of the Lamb and the beast and the church's suffering and victory, its message does not depend on dating. Most idealist commentators nonetheless accept the traditional Domitianic date and read the imperial cult of the 90s as the first instance of a recurring pattern.
note: Disputed. Hendriksen and Milligan favoured the late date. Idealists who adopt the early date do so without changing their method.

statement: Revelation was most likely written c. AD 95. Beale argues that Irenaeus's testimony and the situation of the churches support this date, and he adds that his redemptive-historical, largely idealist reading would be little affected by an earlier one. The book's imagery addressed first-century churches under imperial pressure and also every generation until Christ returns.
note: Disputed. Some eclectic interpreters remain undecided between the two dates.

statement: Romans 11 promises that after the 'fullness of the Gentiles' comes in, 'all Israel will be saved'. This means a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews to Christ, whose 'acceptance' will bring 'life from the dead' to the world. Puritan and Reformed postmillennialists made this hope a mainspring of prayer and missions. Converted Jews join the one church. There is no separate national programme or rebuilt temple.
note: Most postmillennialists since the Puritans hold this view. A minority read 'all Israel' as the whole church, following Calvin.

statement: Anthony Hoekema argued that 'all Israel' is the total number of elect Jews, saved throughout the gospel age alongside the fullness of the Gentiles, rather than a future mass conversion. The promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and his one people. The land promise expands into the inheritance of the new earth. Romans 11 remains a call to hope and mission among Jews in every generation.
note: Amillennialists are divided. Vos, Riddlebarger and others expect a future conversion of large numbers of Jews before the return, while Calvin and others read 'all Israel' as the whole church. All reject a distinct national programme, and Riddlebarger notes that the issue does not decide one's millennial view.

statement: The church is the people of God in which promises to Israel are being fulfilled. Romans 11 nonetheless foresees a future turning of ethnic Israel to its Messiah, probably at or just before his return. Ladd held that this conversion would be into the one body of Christ, not a separate dispensational people.
note: Some historic premillennialists also expect a restoration in the land during the millennium. Others spiritualise the land promises more fully.

statement: God's unconditional covenants with Abraham and David guarantee national Israel a future in the land, under the Messiah's throne, distinct from the church. After the church age and the rapture, a believing remnant of Israel will be saved through the tribulation ('the time of Jacob's trouble'). Christ will then reign from Jerusalem over a restored nation, and Romans 11:26 describes this national salvation.
note: Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) stress that Israel and the church share one kingdom programme while keeping a future for national Israel.

statement: AD 70 was the covenantal judgment on the generation that rejected the Messiah. It ended the old-covenant order but did not end God's purpose for Jews as a people. Many partial preterists, following Romans 11, still expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ within the one church. Others read 'all Israel' as the whole people of God.
note: Postmillennial partial preterists (Gentry, Bahnsen) expect a future conversion. N. T. Wright argues that 'all Israel' is the Messiah's redefined people, Jew and Gentile.

statement: Israel's promised salvation and restoration were completed in the first century. The believing remnant of Jews was saved and joined by Gentiles, and the old covenant passed away with the temple in AD 70. That event consummated the new covenant and the 'redemption' Romans 11:26-27 anticipated. No distinct future remains for ethnic Israel, which stands before God like any other people.
note: Critics answer that Paul links Israel's salvation to the Deliverer's coming and that Romans 11:29 presupposes God's continuing purpose for Israel.

statement: Classical Protestant historicists, including many Puritans, Elliott and Barnes, expected a future conversion of the Jews. They often linked it to the drying of the Euphrates and the fall of the papal and Turkish powers. For many it was a key milestone on the prophetic calendar, sometimes joined to a hope for return to the land.
note: Seventh-day Adventist historicism dissents and holds that the church is spiritual Israel without a distinct future for the nation.

statement: Futurists generally hold that Revelation's 144,000 from the tribes of Israel, the temple and the two witnesses in Jerusalem point to a future end-time role for ethnic Israel. The nation will be the focus of the Antichrist's persecution and will turn to the Messiah at his coming. Prophecy concerning Israel will be fulfilled literally in the last days.
note: Historic-premillennial futurists expect a future conversion of Israel without a distinct dispensational programme, which is the future-mass-conversion position.

statement: Revelation's 'Israel', including the 144,000 and the twelve tribes, is the whole sealed people of God. Paul's 'all Israel' is the full complement of elect Jews brought in throughout the age, not a datable future event. Idealists stress the unity of the one people of God under the Lamb.
note: Idealism is a hermeneutic of Revelation, not a doctrine of Israel. Idealist interpreters' views on Romans 11 vary.

statement: The church, made up of believing Jews and Gentiles, is the end-time Israel in which God's promises are fulfilled. Revelation's 144,000 is the same multitude as the innumerable company, seen from another angle. Many eclectic interpreters still leave room for a future harvest of Jews in line with Romans 11.
note: Eclectic readers range from views close to Hoekema's to an expectation of a future mass conversion. The code shown reflects the common emphasis on the church as true Israel.

statement: Christ has all authority in heaven and on earth, and the Great Commission commands the discipling of the nations. Postmillennialists hold that the commission will succeed. The kingdom grows like the mustard seed and the leaven, the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth, and 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord'. Christ remains enthroned until his enemies are made his footstool, and he returns to a largely Christianised world.
note: Postmillennialists still expect setbacks, persecution and possibly a brief final rebellion (Revelation 20:7-9). Their optimism concerns the long-run trajectory of history.

statement: Amillennialists call their view neither optimistic nor pessimistic but realistic. Wheat and tares grow together until the harvest, the kingdom advances and the gospel bears fruit, and the antithesis with evil persists and intensifies before the end. Hoekema stressed that amillennialism's hope is sure because it rests on Christ's present reign and coming victory, not on trends.
note: Some amillennialists lean optimistic about the gospel's spread, and others expect a sharper final apostasy and tribulation.

statement: The gospel will be preached to all nations and the church will grow, but the age ends in tribulation, apostasy and Antichrist's persecution. The church goes through that tribulation. Christ's personal return, not the church's gradual success, brings in the era of earthly peace and justice in the millennium.
note: Historic premillennialists are often hopeful about missions and the church's witness. Their 'pessimism' concerns the world-system before the return.

statement: Scripture forecasts that the church age ends in apostasy and 'perilous times'. The church's mission is to evangelise individuals, not to Christianise society. The church will be raptured before the tribulation, and the world will be restored only when Christ returns to reign for a thousand years. Dispensationalists call this hope 'the blessed hope' and present it as comforting, not gloomy.
note: Dispensationalists reject the label 'pessimist'. They hold that God's plan is succeeding exactly as prophesied.

statement: Because the great tribulation and the judgments of the Olivet Discourse and much of Revelation fell on first-century Jerusalem, no future great tribulation hangs over the church. The 'last days' of the old covenant ended in AD 70. The rest of history is the era of the gospel's expanding kingdom under the reigning Christ.
note: Most partial preterists are postmillennial. Amillennial partial preterists (Jay Adams, many followers of Sproul) take the amillennial 'realistic' stance.

statement: Since every prophecy was fulfilled by AD 70, the kingdom is fully established and Christ reigns now without rival. Many full preterists hold that history has no final end. The kingdom grows without limit, 'of the increase of his government there shall be no end', and believers live in the new covenant age that never closes.
note: Some full preterists make no predictions about the course of history. Critics note that denying any future consummation of history sits outside creedal orthodoxy.

statement: In the classic Reformation and Puritan form, historicists read history through Revelation as the progressive overthrow of Antichrist (the papacy) and the Turk, followed by a latter-day glory of the gospel. Edwards and the Puritan postmillennialists built their missionary hope on this reading of prophecy.
note: Historicists are divided. Many nineteenth-century historicists (Elliott, Guinness) were premillennial and expected decline before the return, and Seventh-day Adventist historicism is strongly premillennial.

statement: Revelation 6-19 lies ahead and describes an unprecedented end-time tribulation, so history moves toward a climactic crisis before Christ intervenes. Futurists still consider the believer's hope bright, because it rests on the return of the King, who personally ends evil.
note: Futurism is a hermeneutic, so its stance on optimism follows its adherents' millennial views. Most futurists are premillennial: dispensationalists expect apostasy and a pretribulational rapture, while historic premillennialists expect the church to endure the tribulation.

statement: Revelation's cycles show the same pattern in every generation. The church suffers and conquers, the beast rages and is defeated, and the Lamb is always on the throne. History does not trend steadily up or down. It is the stage on which the conflict of the two cities repeats until Christ comes.
note: Idealism is compatible with several millennial views. Idealist postmillennialists are optimistic, idealist amillennialists are 'realistic', and idealist premillennialists expect a final crisis.

statement: The 'already/not yet' runs through the church's whole history. Christ has already won, the church already reigns and witnesses, and the same age is marked by tribulation and opposition that will intensify in a final rebellion before the end. Eclectic interpreters such as Beale are therefore neither triumphalist nor despairing about history before the return.
note: Most eclectic readers are amillennial, though some premillennial interpreters (e.g. Osborne) use the method.

statement: The kingdom was inaugurated at Christ's first coming and enthroned at his ascension. It now grows by Word and Spirit, like the stone that becomes a great mountain and the leaven that works through the whole lump. Christ reigns from heaven until all enemies are subdued. The kingdom will transform hearts, families, cultures and nations before its consummation at his return.
note: Postmillennialists differ on how much the kingdom affects civil institutions. Theonomic postmillennialists expect it to shape civil law, and others focus on revival and cultural influence.

statement: The kingdom is 'already and not yet'. Christ reigns now at the Father's right hand, the saints reign with him (Revelation 20:4-6 describes the intermediate state and the church's present reign), and the kingdom advances through the gospel. Its full, visible form comes only with the return, the general resurrection and the new heavens and new earth. No earthly millennium intervenes.

Ladd's 'presence of the future' holds that God's reign broke in with Jesus and is present now in power. Its manifestation in history will come in two further stages: a thousand-year earthly reign after the return (Revelation 20:4-6), and then the eternal kingdom in the new creation. The millennium vindicates Christ's lordship within history itself.

Jesus offered Israel the promised Davidic kingdom. When the nation rejected him, its establishment was postponed, and the present age is a 'mystery form' of the kingdom in which the church is formed. At his return Christ will sit on David's throne in Jerusalem and rule the earth for a literal thousand years, fulfilling the land and throne promises.
note: Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock) hold that the Davidic throne is already inaugurated with Christ at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-36), an already/not yet close to historic premillennialism.

statement: The kingdom came 'with power' within the lifetime of some who heard Jesus (Mark 9:1). It was inaugurated at the resurrection and ascension and publicly vindicated when the old-covenant order fell in AD 70. Christ now reigns, and the unshakeable kingdom that replaced the shaken one advances through history toward the final consummation.
note: Amillennial partial preterists use the inaugurated-consummated framework without the postmillennial growth expectation. N. T. Wright stresses the kingdom's arrival in Jesus' work and vindication.

statement: Jesus promised the kingdom within that generation. At the Parousia in AD 70 the kingdom was fully established, the old age ended and the age to come began. Believers now live in the consummated kingdom, which is spiritual, eternal and ever-present. There is no future coming or end of history to wait for.
note: Critics from all other schools reply that this denies the future bodily return and resurrection confessed in the historic creeds.

statement: Classical historicists saw Christ's kingdom as present in his church through history, fighting the Antichrist powers, and to be consummated at his coming. Revelation traces that struggle from the first century to the end. Most Reformers held a broadly Augustinian view of the present kingdom.
note: Historicists span every millennial view. Puritan historicists were often postmillennial, and Elliott and Seventh-day Adventists are premillennial. Adventists place the millennium in heaven, with the earth desolate.

statement: Most futurists expect Revelation 19-20 to be fulfilled literally after Christ's return. He will establish a visible kingdom on earth for a thousand years before the eternal state. The promises to David and the prophets' pictures of a renewed earth await this future reign.
note: Historic-premillennial futurists hold inaugurated-plus-millennial and do not use the 'postponement' language.

statement: The Lamb's victory is already won and his kingdom is present wherever the saints overcome. Revelation repeatedly unveils Christ enthroned over history. The thousand years symbolise the whole gospel age of Christ's reign and Satan's restraint, and the final chapters picture its consummation in the new creation.
note: Most idealists are amillennial. A few combine idealism with postmillennial growth.

statement: Christ's death and resurrection inaugurated the end-time kingdom, and believers already reign as a kingdom of priests even while they suffer. The kingdom will be consummated at his return in the new heavens and earth. Beale describes this as 'inaugurated eschatology' running through the whole New Testament.
note: Premillennial eclectic interpreters add a future millennial phase.

statement: At the close of history Christ returns once, raises all the dead, righteous and wicked together, and judges all people in one general judgment. The eternal state follows. Postmillennialists hold this in line with the Westminster Confession and see no thousand-year gap between resurrections, since 'an hour is coming' when all in the tombs come forth.

One Second Coming brings one general resurrection and one general judgment of all, followed by the new heavens and earth. The 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20 is spiritual (regeneration or the soul's entrance into heaven), not a separate bodily resurrection. The Great White Throne is therefore the same event as the judgment in Matthew 25.

At his return Christ raises believers in the 'first resurrection' to reign with him. 'The rest of the dead' are raised after the thousand years for judgment at the Great White Throne. John 5:28-29 speaks of two resurrections without specifying their timing, and Revelation 20 supplies the interval.
note: Historic premillennialists differ on whether believers also stand at the Great White Throne.

statement: Scripture distinguishes several judgments. Church-age believers are rewarded at the judgment seat of Christ after the rapture. Israel is judged at the end of the tribulation, and the living Gentile nations at the sheep-and-goats judgment as the millennium begins. After the thousand years the unbelieving dead are judged at the Great White Throne. Each judgment differs in subject, time and basis.
note: The detailed list varies between authors. Some also include a judgment of tribulation and Old Testament saints at the return.

statement: AD 70 was a historical judgment-coming of Christ on Jerusalem, but it was not the final judgment. Partial preterists confess, with the creeds, a future bodily return, a general resurrection and a last judgment of all people. Texts such as Acts 17:31 and 1 Corinthians 15 point beyond the first century.
note: Partial preterists differ on which texts refer to AD 70 and which to the final judgment, especially Matthew 25:31-46.

statement: The resurrection and judgment Jesus and the apostles said were 'about to' happen (Acts 24:15 'mellein', 2 Timothy 4:1) took place at his coming in AD 70. Most full preterists understand the resurrection as corporate and covenantal, the raising of God's people from the 'death' of the old covenant, rather than a resurrection of physical corpses. Since then, individuals pass into judgment at death.
note: This position lies outside historic creedal orthodoxy, which confesses a future return 'to judge the living and the dead' and a resurrection of the body. Critics argue that it collapses the physical resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15. Proponents answer that the creeds must yield to the biblical time texts.

statement: Classical Protestant historicists, following the Reformation confessions, expected Christ's single return at the end of the prophetic sequence, a general resurrection and the last judgment. Revelation's prophetic chain ends with the Great White Throne and the new creation.
note: Premillennial historicists (Elliott, Guinness) held two resurrections. Seventh-day Adventists teach a pre-advent 'investigative judgment' beginning in 1844, the righteous raised at the return, and the wicked raised and destroyed after a millennium in heaven.

statement: Revelation 4-22 describes a future sequence: judgments on the earth during the tribulation, Christ's return to judge the beast and the nations, the thousand-year reign, and finally the Great White Throne. Futurists read these as distinct events in sequence.
note: Historic-premillennial futurists hold a simpler two-resurrection scheme (two-stage-premil) without the separate believers' and nations' judgments.

statement: Revelation's cycles each end with a picture of the final judgment, the same event seen from different angles (Revelation 6:12-17, Revelation 11:15-18, Revelation 14:14-20, Revelation 20:11-15). They are not separate judgments in sequence. At the one return of Christ all are judged according to their works.
note: Idealists who are premillennial (a small minority) hold two resurrections.

statement: Revelation recapitulates: several visions climax in the same last judgment. The Great White Throne is the single final judgment of all the dead at Christ's return. Beale argues that the 'second death' and 'first resurrection' contrast spiritual and physical realities rather than two bodily resurrections.
note: Eclectic interpreters who are premillennial hold two resurrections.

statement: Postmillennialists trace their hope to patristic confidence in the gospel's triumph (Eusebius, Athanasius) and to Calvin's optimism about Christ's kingdom. It became a full eschatology among the Puritans and Scottish Covenanters. It shaped the Great Awakening (Jonathan Edwards), the modern missionary movement and Old Princeton (Hodge, Warfield), and it was arguably the dominant American Protestant view in the nineteenth century. After a twentieth-century eclipse it revived through Boettner, Murray and the Reformed and theonomic movements.
note: Postmillennialists dispute whether the patristic and Reformation figures they cite were truly postmillennial. Critics link the view's decline to the world wars, and proponents reply that theology should not follow headlines.

statement: Amillennialists trace their view to Tyconius and especially Augustine (City of God XX), who read Revelation 20 as the church's present reign. From the fifth century through the Reformation this was the church's majority view. Lutheran and Reformed confessions reflect it. Today it is widely held across Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican, Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions.
note: The term 'amillennial' is modern (twentieth century). Some argue that Augustine's view is equally an ancestor of postmillennialism.

statement: Historic premillennialists claim the earliest post-apostolic witnesses. Papias, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and Tertullian expected a literal reign of Christ on earth after the resurrection of the righteous. The name 'historic' signals this patristic pedigree. The view waned after Augustine, reappeared among some Puritans (Joseph Mede) and was revived in the twentieth century by George Ladd.
note: Justin himself admitted that some orthodox Christians did not share his chiliasm, so how widely early chiliasm was held is debated.

statement: Dispensationalism as a system arose with J. N. Darby and the Brethren in the 1830s. It spread through the Bible and prophecy conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and Dallas Theological Seminary, and became the dominant view of twentieth-century American evangelicalism. Proponents argue that its premillennialism and literal hermeneutic recover the early church's chiliasm, and that the newness of its systematisation no more discredits it than the late formulation of other doctrines.
note: Dispensationalists point to patristic and later precedents for elements such as imminence. Critics stress the novelty of the pretribulational rapture and the Israel/church distinction.

statement: Partial preterists point to Eusebius, who read the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled in AD 70 from Josephus's history, and to Chrysostom. Revelation was systematically interpreted preteristically by the Jesuit Luis de Alcázar (1614) and Protestants such as Hugo Grotius, Henry Hammond and John Lightfoot. Moses Stuart and Milton Terry developed it further, and since the 1980s it has revived through Chilton, Gentry, DeMar and Sproul.
note: Opponents emphasise the Counter-Reformation origin of systematic preterism. Proponents reply that the AD 70 reading of the Olivet Discourse is patristic and widespread among Reformed commentators.

statement: As a full system, full preterism (also called 'consistent' or 'covenant eschatology') is recent. J. Stuart Russell's The Parousia (1878) argued that every New Testament prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, and the modern movement grew from Max King's work in the 1970s, carried on by writers such as Don Preston. Proponents say they are recovering the apostles' own time-frame, which the church lost.
note: Critics point out that no church father, council or confession held the view and that it contradicts the creeds' future return and resurrection. Proponents answer with sola Scriptura.

statement: Historicism has roots in Joachim of Fiore's twelfth-century periodisation of history and in medieval dissenters. It became the standard Protestant reading at the Reformation, when Luther, the Reformed and the Westminster divines identified the papacy as Antichrist. Isaac Newton, Puritan expositors, Jonathan Edwards, Albert Barnes and E. B. Elliott continued it, and it dominated until the mid-nineteenth century. Today it is maintained chiefly by Seventh-day Adventists and some confessional Protestants.
note: Its decline is often traced to failed date-setting (e.g. Millerism in 1844) and to the rise of futurism and critical scholarship.

statement: Futurists point to Irenaeus and Hippolytus, who expected a future personal Antichrist and a literal three-and-a-half-year tribulation. Systematic futurism was developed by the Jesuit Francisco Ribera (c. 1590) and Cardinal Bellarmine, partly in answer to Protestant historicism. Protestant writers (S. R. Maitland, J. H. Todd, Darby) revived it in the nineteenth century, and it is now the most popular popular-level reading.
note: Historicist critics have used Ribera's Jesuit role polemically. Futurists respond that their view stands or falls on exegesis, and they claim the early fathers' expectation of a future Antichrist as precedent.

statement: The spiritual or symbolic reading of Revelation goes back to the Alexandrian tradition (Origen) and above all to Tyconius and Augustine. Their non-chronological, recapitulating reading of the Apocalypse governed much of the medieval church. Modern idealism was articulated by William Milligan (1886) and popularised in Reformed circles by Hendriksen.
note: Idealism as a named 'school' is a modern category. Its patristic roots are shared with amillennialism.

statement: The eclectic approach is a late twentieth-century development in evangelical scholarship, best represented by G. K. Beale's 1999 commentary and followed by others such as Grant Osborne and Craig Keener. It deliberately combines the idealist core with preterist attention to the first-century setting and a futurist consummation, and so draws on every older stream of interpretation.
note: Proponents note that patristic commentators already mixed historical, symbolic and future readings, so eclecticism is arguably older than its label.
